title: Nested requirements files can expand exponentially
body:
### Description

`RequirementsFileParser._parse_and_recurse` tracks already-seen files per chain of
includes (`parsed_files_stack[0]`), not globally. A requirements file reached through
several chains is therefore parsed once per chain, which is deliberate (#13046,
#13047) — a file may legitimately be included more than once.

The consequence is that the number of files parsed grows with the number of *paths*
through the include graph rather than its size. A file that includes the same child
twice at every level doubles the work for each level of nesting, and nothing bounds
the total.

### Reproduction

Create `f0.txt` … `f{n-1}.txt`, each containing `-r f{i+1}.txt` twice, and a leaf
`f{n}.txt` with one requirement:

```python
import os, sys
d = int(sys.argv[1]); out = sys.argv[2]
os.makedirs(out, exist_ok=True)
for i in range(d):
    open(f"{out}/f{i}.txt", "w").write(f"-r f{i+1}.txt\n-r f{i+1}.txt\n")
open(f"{out}/f{d}.txt", "w").write("requests\n")
```

Then `pip install --dry-run --no-deps --no-index -r f0.txt` (`--no-index` so the
timing is parsing only; the expansion happens before anything is downloaded):

| files | bytes total | time |
|---|---|---|
| 11 | 211 | 0.60 s |
| 13 | 255 | 1.73 s |
| 15 | 299 | 6.31 s |
| 17 | 343 | 28.49 s |
| 19 | 387 | 136.16 s |

Baseline for a single requirement is 0.26 s. Each further level multiplies the time
by about 4.8, so roughly 650 bytes of requirements files extrapolates to days of CPU
time. The expansion is also why the ratio exceeds the theoretical 4x — the per-chain
dictionaries are copied at every level.

### Why I think it is worth bounding

The cost is paid while parsing, before anything is downloaded or built, so it also
applies to flows that never run package code (`--dry-run`, `download --no-deps`).
That makes it relevant wherever a requirements file is less trusted than the machine
installing it — CI running `pip install -r` against a pull request, or an automated
dependency job.

I don't believe this is a security issue under `SECURITY.md` (a requirements file is
neither a package nor an index, and the expansion happens before any step that runs
arbitrary code), which is why I am filing it here rather than mailing
security@python.org. Happy to be told otherwise.

### Versions

Measured on pip 24.2, 26.2.2 and `main`. pip 24.3 is **not** affected — it rejects
the input immediately with "recursively references itself" — but that is the version
whose global tracking rejected legitimate DAGs, which is what #13046 reported and
#13047 fixed. So this is not a regression from #13047; 24.2 and earlier behave the
same as today.

I have a patch that bounds the total number of nested files parsed, leaving the
shape of the include graph (and therefore #13046) untouched, and will open a PR.

title: Previously authenticated HTTP response returned for unauthenticated HTTP request
body:
### Description

A system configuration test case that ensured `python -m pip index versions pip` returned no results for a user account without `.netrc` authentication configured failed by appearing to get a valid response from an internal index server that requires mandatory user authentication.

`PIP_INDEX_URL` was NOT defined at the time of the test execution, but the user account under test had been recently executing commands with valid credentials provided via `PIP_INDEX_URL`, so there would have been a valid HTTP cache entry for the `pip` version listing request. The test is running in a container emulating a server environment _without_ `keyring` configured and with `/etc/pip.conf` defaulting to anonymous access, so `.netrc` and `PIP_INDEX_URL` are the only potential sources of authentication details.

Running `python -m pip index versions pip` after the configure-and-test run finished failed as expected.
Changing the test command to `python -m pip index --no-cache-dir versions pip` also failed as expected.

(since the HTTP cache is stored in a user-specific directory, I don't consider this to be a security problem - the only way the caching discrepancy can come up is for a single user to be intentionally switching between authenticated and unauthenticated access, or authentication with different accounts, and either way, it's all information that the local user account is authorised to access)

### Expected behavior

Given an index server with mandatory authentication requirements and valid credentials in `.netrc`, running:

```
python3.11 -m pip index versions pip
rm ~/.netrc
python3.11 -m pip index versions pip
```

should result in the second command reporting `ERROR: No matching distribution found for pip` rather than the previously cached authenticated response (and similarly if the credentials were originally supplied via `PIP_INDEX_URL` or any other mechanism).

### pip version

26.2.1

### Python version

3.11.15

### OS

Linux

### How to Reproduce

1. Configure the default index server to be one that requires authentication
2. Run `pip index versions pip` with valid credentials (however supplied)
3. Run `pip index versions pip` *without* valid credentials (but within the HTTP cache validity window)

The last command will still get a HTTP cache hit, even though the user authentication details have changed.

title: https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/new/choose
Constraint hash ignored for a transitively-needed package given in URL form
body:
Found while implementing `pylock.toml` support for `-c`/`--constraint`/`--build-constraint`
(see #13961) — mentioned there for context, not filed as a duplicate.

## Description

When a package is only needed transitively (pulled in by another requirement's own
dependency, not requested directly) and its version/hash is pinned via a constraint
given in URL form (`name @ url --hash=...`), the hash from the constraint is not
applied to the resolved candidate. Instead of using it, `--require-hashes` mode reports
the hash as **missing** — even though the constraint file clearly provides one.

This is because `_iter_candidates_from_constraints()` in
`src/pip/_internal/resolution/resolvelib/factory.py` builds the candidate for such a
package via `install_req_from_link_and_ireq(link, template)`, where `template` is the
*requirement that pulled the package in* (e.g. `requests`' own `certifi>=2017.4.17`),
not the constraint. `install_req_from_link_and_ireq()` copies `hash_options` from that
template, which has none — so the resulting candidate ends up with no hash at all,
regardless of what the constraint specified.

This code path is only taken when `constraint.links` is non-empty, i.e. when the
constraint uses the URL form. Classic `name==version --hash=...` constraint lines never
populate `.link`, so they take a different, correct path
(`_iter_found_candidates()`, which does use `constraint.hash_options`) and are
unaffected. It's specifically the URL form that's broken.

## Is URL-form even a supported constraint form?

`check_invalid_constraint_type()` (`src/pip/_internal/req/req_install.py`) explicitly
rejects only three constraint forms: unnamed, editable, and extras — URL form
(`name @ url`) is not among them. It's also actively covered by
`test_new_resolver_hash_requirement_and_url_constraint_can_succeed`/`_can_fail` in
`tests/functional/test_new_resolver_hashes.py`, which confirm it works correctly
**when the same package is also required directly** (in that case the requirement's own
hash covers it, and this bug never triggers). This report is about the previously
untested case where the constrained package is *only* pulled in transitively — not
about whether URL-form constraints should be allowed at all.

## Expected behavior

The hash from the constraint should be applied to the resolved candidate, exactly as it
is when the same package is required directly (not just pulled in transitively) — or
when the constraint uses the classic `--hash=` form instead of URL form.

## pip version

26.2.1 (also present on `main`, unfixed at the time of writing — this predates any of
the `pylock.toml`-constraint work in #13961)

## Python version

3.13.14

## OS

Linux

## How to Reproduce

1. `requirements.txt` — only requires `requests` directly:
   ```
   requests==2.32.5
   ```
2. `constraints.txt` — pins all four of `requests`' dependencies; `certifi` (purely
   transitive, never requested directly) is given in URL form, the other three in
   classic hash form:
   ```
   requests==2.32.5 --hash=sha256:2462f94637a34fd532264295e186976db0f5d453d1cdd31473c85a6a161affb6
   charset-normalizer==3.5.1 --hash=sha256:62b55f6722735a6c472f88361cde6640608773d9443cebdbb51abf436a1fcdd3
   idna==3.19 --hash=sha256:815e7be7a7806d54abb586dc943addc79e8b2ee16915059658cbeff4b1b43bf4
   urllib3==2.7.0 --hash=sha256:9fb4c81ebbb1ce9531cce37674bbc6f1360472bc18ca9a553ede278ef7276897
   certifi @ https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/0b/a7/71ac2cff56fec219ed242bb11b8efb69fcc4bec75db06fb7bfe35de520e6/certifi-2026.7.22-py3-none-any.whl --hash=sha256:62f22742b58a1a33014a2b6b706588a8d7e2a88ae7bd1a6ebe8c992928483775
   ```
3. Run:
   ```
   pip install -r requirements.txt -c constraints.txt
   ```

## Output

```
$ pip install -r requirements.txt -c constraints.txt --dry-run
Collecting requests==2.32.5 (from -r requirements.txt (line 1))
  Using cached requests-2.32.5-py3-none-any.whl (64 kB)
Collecting charset_normalizer==3.5.1 (from requests==2.32.5->-r requirements.txt (line 1))
  Using cached charset_normalizer-3.5.1-cp313-cp313-manylinux2014_x86_64.manylinux_2_17_x86_64.manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl (250 kB)
Collecting idna==3.19 (from requests==2.32.5->-r requirements.txt (line 1))
  Using cached idna-3.19-py3-none-any.whl (68 kB)
Collecting urllib3==2.7.0 (from requests==2.32.5->-r requirements.txt (line 1))
  Using cached urllib3-2.7.0-py3-none-any.whl (131 kB)
Collecting certifi>=2017.4.17 (from requests==2.32.5->-r requirements.txt (line 1))
  Using cached certifi-2026.7.22-py3-none-any.whl (136 kB)
ERROR: Hashes are required in --require-hashes mode, but they are missing from some requirements. Here is a list of those requirements along with the hashes their downloaded archives actually had. Add lines like these to your requirements files to prevent tampering. (If you did not enable --require-hashes manually, note that it turns on automatically when any package has a hash.)
    https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/0b/a7/71ac2cff56fec219ed242bb11b8efb69fcc4bec75db06fb7bfe35de520e6/certifi-2026.7.22-py3-none-any.whl --hash=sha256:62f22742b58a1a33014a2b6b706588a8d7e2a88ae7bd1a6ebe8c992928483775
```

Note the hash pip suggests adding is the *exact same hash already present* in
`constraints.txt` — it was available, just never consulted.

## Fix

Have a fix ready: fall back to the constraint's own `hash_options` in
`_iter_candidates_from_constraints()` when the template requirement has none, mirroring
what `_iter_found_candidates()` already does on the sibling path. Opening a PR
referencing this issue shortly. The `pylock.toml`-as-constraint feature from #13961
depends on this fix, since `pylock.toml` wheel/sdist entries are structurally always
URL-form and trigger it reliably — that feature is a separate PR.

title: Warn/default-abort when installing conflicting packages
body:
### What's the problem this feature will solve?

Naming collisions, while undesireable, do exist. `pip` could avoid making that problem worse -- currently it will happily try to install both packages on top of each other, creating an incoherent mess.

### Describe the solution you'd like

When asked to install two packages containing modules by the same name, `pip` should either warn or abort-by-default (perhaps leaving an escape hatch if someone knows what they're doing). Depending on the amount of metadata available to pip, this might only be possible when `pip` is already trying to unpack the wheel, but hopefully this can be done before any file is extracted.

### Alternative Solutions

- Strengthen PyPI policies against uploading colliding names -- likely expensive.
- Do nothing given this is relatively rare -- but the resulting bugs are hard to diagnose

### Additional context

One case where this comes up is when a PEP-541 request takes a while to process, so the original and new project exist simultaneously. In particular, this bit me with https://github.com/pypi/support/issues/9590

title: pip should understand forward and/or double backslashes in the paths inside OpenSSL config files on MS-Windows
body:
### What's the problem this feature will solve? Hi, On an MS-Windows machine I configured `OpenSSL` by putting these lines into its config file:
OpenSSL config: 
openssl_conf = openssl_def

[openssl_def]
engines = engine_section

[engine_section]
gost = gost_section

[gost_section]
engine_id = gost
dynamic_path = C:/Program Files/OpenSSL-Win64/engines/gost.dll
default_algorithms = ALL
After that `pip` started reporting "NID creation failed" in the first line of its output. Looks like that happens because `pip` doesn't understand forward slashes (`/`) in the line `dynamic_path = C:/Program Files/OpenSSL-Win64/engines/gost.dll`. I tried replacing the forward slashes with double backslashes (`\\`), but `pip` still reported the error. Then I tried replacing them with single backslashes (`\`), and `pip` stopped reporting the error, but this time `OpenSSL` itself didn't see the path. ### Describe the solution you'd like Perhaps `pip` should understand forward and/or double backslashes in this situation. ### Alternative Solutions None. ### Additional context OS: Windows 10 Home 22H2, Python v. 3.13.15, pip v. 26.2.1, OpenSSL v. 3.5.7. ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow the [PSF Code of Conduct](https://www.python.org/psf/conduct/).

title: pip list outdated does not respect --uploaded-prior-to option
body:
## Description

`pip list --outdated --uploaded-prior-to=<duration>` does not respect the
`--uploaded-prior-to` cooldown filter when determining the "Latest" version
of a package. It reports a version that was uploaded well *within* the
cooldown window as the latest available version.

By contrast, `pip install --dry-run --uploaded-prior-to=<duration>` (and by
extension `pip download`) correctly resolves to the newest version that
satisfies the cooldown constraint. This inconsistency suggests that
`pip list --outdated` uses a different code path for latest-version
resolution that does not apply the upload-time filter.

## Expected behavior

`pip list --outdated --uploaded-prior-to=P60D` should report the same
"Latest" version for a package as
`pip install --dry-run --uploaded-prior-to=P60D <package>` would resolve to
— i.e., only versions uploaded at least 60 days ago should be considered
candidates for "Latest".

## How to Reproduce

Using a package with several releases in the last ~60 days (example below
uses the PyPI package `ae-base`, but any actively-maintained package on PyPI with recent
releases should reproduce this):

1. Check today's date and the upload times of the package's releases via
   the Simple Repository API (PEP 700):

   ```console
   $ date
   Sun 19 Jul 2026 15:32:20 WEST

   $ curl -s -H "Accept: application/vnd.pypi.simple.v1+json" \
       https://pypi.org/simple/ae-base/ | python -m json.tool | grep -i upload
               ...
               "upload-time": "2026-06-28T15:51:35.940403Z",
   ```

   The most recent upload (`0.3.89`) was made on 2026-06-28, only 21 days
   before "today" — well inside a 60-day cooldown window.

2. Run `pip list --outdated` with a 60-day cooldown:

   ```console
   $ pip list --outdated --uploaded-prior-to=P60D
   Package     Version  Latest  Type
   ----------- -------- ------- -----
   ae-base     0.3.87   0.3.89  wheel
   ```

   `0.3.89` is reported as "Latest" even though it was uploaded only 21 days
   ago — it should have been excluded by `--uploaded-prior-to=P60D`.

3. Run the equivalent resolution via `pip install --dry-run` for
   comparison:

   ```console
   $ pip install --dry-run --ignore-installed --uploaded-prior-to=P60D ae-base
   Collecting ae_base
     Downloading ae_base-0.3.83-py3-none-any.whl.metadata (5.2 kB)
   Would install ae_base-0.3.83
   ```

   Here pip correctly resolves to `0.3.83`, a version uploaded before the
   60-day cutoff — as expected.

   `pip cache purge` was run beforehand to rule out caching effects.

## pip version

26.1.2

## Python version

3.12.12

## OS

Linux

## Additional context

This was found while building tooling around "dependency cooldowns" that
relies on `pip list --outdated --uploaded-prior-to=...` to determine which
installed packages have a cooldown-eligible update available. Because
`pip list --outdated` silently ignores the cooldown filter for "Latest"
resolution, packages are incorrectly reported as outdated even when no
cooldown-compliant update actually exists yet (as confirmed by the
`pip install --dry-run` control test above).

title: pip `--no-input` disables credential extraction from redirect URLs, breaking downloads behind auth-redirecting indexes
body:
### Description
I encountered an unexpected behavior when using `pip download` using `uv run --no-project --with python -m pip`. There was a strange behavior where I find out somehow `--no-input` affect the result of auth.

## Contexet

Download/install a package from a private index that answers with a 302 redirect whose Location carries embedded Basic-auth credentials (https://user:token@upstream/...) — a common setup with devpi in front of Artifactory/JFrog, and similar proxy configurations — while passing --no-input (e.g. in CI).

## What happened

The download fails with 401 Unauthorized, but only when `--no-input` is used. The exact same command without `--no-input` succeeds.

## Root cause

When an index issues a cross-origin 302, the vendored requests session strips the Authorization header (should_strip_auth), so the upstream host receives no credentials and returns 401. pip's handle_401 (src/pip/_internal/network/auth.py) is supposed to recover: the embedded credentials are still present in resp.url, and _get_new_credentials() extracts URL-embedded credentials before it ever touches keyring or prompts.

### Expected behavior

`--no-input` shouldn't affect authentication and expect same behavior.

### pip version

25.3

### Python version

3.13

### OS

MacOS/Linux

### How to Reproduce

When an index issues a cross-origin 302, the vendored requests session strips the Authorization header (should_strip_auth), so the upstream host receives no credentials and returns 401. pip's handle_401 (src/pip/_internal/network/auth.py) is supposed to recover: the embedded credentials are still present in resp.url, and _get_new_credentials() extracts URL-embedded credentials before it ever touches keyring or prompts.

The problem is that this recovery call is gated behind use_keyring:
```python
# src/pip/_internal/network/auth.py, handle_401()
username, password = None, None

# Query the keyring for credentials:
if self.use_keyring:                       # <-- gate
    username, password = self._get_new_credentials(
        resp.url,
        allow_netrc=False,
        allow_keyring=True,
    )

if not self.prompting and not username and not password:
    return resp                            # <-- returns the 401 unretriedreturns the 401.
```
--no-input is documented as "Disable prompting for input", but it also silently disables this non-interactive redirect-credential recovery.

## Minimal reproduction

This example is generated with AI, but I did test it to confirm the behavior is same as what I experience.

Self-contained, stdlib + pip only (no external index needed). Two local servers stand in for "index → upstream"; only auth.prompting (what --no-input sets) differs between the two attempts:
```python
import base64, threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from pip._internal.network.auth import MultiDomainBasicAuth
from pip._vendor import requests

USER, TOKEN = "user", "token"
EXPECTED = "Basic " + base64.b64encode(f"{USER}:{TOKEN}".encode()).decode()

class Upstream(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.headers.get("Authorization") == EXPECTED:
            self.send_response(200); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b"OK")
        else:
            self.send_response(401)
            self.send_header("WWW-Authenticate", 'Basic realm="x"'); self.end_headers()
    def log_message(self, *a): pass

def index(location):
    class Index(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def do_GET(self):
            self.send_response(302); self.send_header("Location", location); self.end_headers()
        def log_message(self, *a): pass
    return Index

def serve(handler):
    srv = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), handler)
    threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
    return srv.server_address[1]

def attempt(prompting):
    port_b = serve(Upstream)                                  # upstream (127.0.0.1)
    port_a = serve(index(f"http://{USER}:{TOKEN}@127.0.0.1:{port_b}/pkg"))  # index (localhost)
    url = f"http://localhost:{port_a}/"
    s = requests.Session()
    s.auth = MultiDomainBasicAuth(prompting=prompting, index_urls=[url])
    return s.get(url, timeout=5).status_code
Both attempts return 200. Extracting credentials embedded in a redirect URL requires no user interaction, so --no-input should not disable it.
```

### Output

default   (prompting=True) : 200
--no-input(prompting=False): 401

title: Add a `--no-require-hashes` option
body:
I propose to add a `--no-require-hashes` option.

Currently, as soon as pip encounters a requirement with hashes, it activates the `--require-hashes` option. This prevents combining hash requirements with other requirements provided as direct URLs.

This is problem is described in #4995 and #6469, and propagates to -r pylock.toml in #13943 and #13944.

To solve these issues, I had started drafting a PR #11968 to accept VCS direct URLs with immutable commit hash in require hashes mode. I was also thinking about trusting local directories direct URLs in require hashes mode.

Both could be seen as breaking changes, though.

Then I looked at what uv chose to do with this and I notice they do not auto-enable `--require-hashes`. This allows for both use cases: 1/ allow combining hashed reqs and direct URLs and letting the user take responsibility over their requirement files (which is probably fine in many cases, as requirement files with hashes are generated by tools) 2/ enable `--require-hashes`, rejecting direct URLs.

So I now consider adding `--no-require-hashes` to pip, enabling the same combinations, albeit with a different default.

title: Extend regression test on self-referential extras
body:
## Context After https://github.com/pypa/pip/pull/14157, self-referential extras is now documented as an official feature (supported unofficially [since v21.2](https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/10393#issuecomment-941885429)), #14157 also introduced two simple test cases into `tests/functional/test_install_extras.py`: - `test_install_self_referential_extras[separate-specifiers]` - `test_install_self_referential_extras[combined-specifier]` The test cases were quite simple - in fact they pass with `v20.3 - v21.1.3`. ## Proposal Add 9 more test cases to cover expected behaviour and prevent regression. ### Should pass with 20.3+ 1. **nested** — nested self-referential extras should work. 2. **external** — a self-referential extra can mix `pkg[a]` with an unrelated third-party dep in the same extra. 3. **partial** — after `pkg[a]` is already installed, installing `pkg[all]` with the same version adds only the missing deps. 4. **unknown** — a self-reference with unknown extra (`pkg[missing]`) must raise a warning as usual. 5. **upgrade-dep** — a self-referential extra whose dependency version requirements change across versions (from requiring `dep==1` to requiring `dep==2`) must bump `dep` to version 2. 6. **circular** — mutually dependent extras (extra `a` depends on extra `b` and vice versa) must resolve normally (`pip install pkg[a]` installs dependencies from both extras). ### Should pass with 21.2+ 7 & 8. **upgrade-different-extras** (two scenarios: had-no-extra or had-different-extras) — with an older pkg already installed (with no extras defined or with different extras defined and installed), upgrading to a new version with an `all` extra should: 1) pull new deps and 2) downgrade an existing dep. ### Should pass with 24.1+ 9. **normalize** — PEP 685 normalization should allow `"all": ["pkg[x-y]"]` to install extra defined as `x_y` in `pyproject.toml`. ## Local Test Results

Runs the real tests from tests/functional/test_install_extras.py against each pip version by swapping the pip installed into the test virtualenv template. Usage: nox -f noxfile_self_ref_extras.py nox -f noxfile_self_ref_extras.py -- 21.2 26.1.2 """ import json import os import shutil import tempfile import urllib.request from pathlib import Path import nox from packaging.version import InvalidVersion, Version ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent MIN_VERSION = Version("20.2") # Old pip needs pkgutil.ImpImporter (removed in 3.12). PEP685_MIN = Version("24.1") NORM_TEST = "test_install_self_referential_extras_name_normalization" nox.options.sessions = ["self_ref_extras"] nox.options.reuse_existing_virtualenvs = True # Pytest plugin loaded via -p: replace HEAD pip in the test venv with a # historical release. Kept inline so this experiment is a single file. # Network is blocked under pytest (pytest-subket); wheels are pre-downloaded # by the nox session into SELF_REF_EXTRAS_WHEELHOUSE. _PLUGIN = r""" import os import shutil import subprocess import sys from pathlib import Path import pytest @pytest.fixture(scope="session", autouse=True) def _swap_historical_pip(virtualenv_template): version = os.environ["SELF_REF_EXTRAS_PIP_VERSION"] wheelhouse = os.environ["SELF_REF_EXTRAS_WHEELHOUSE"] site = Path(virtualenv_template.site) for path in list(site.glob("*pip*.pth")) + list(site.glob("__editable__*pip*")): if path.is_dir(): shutil.rmtree(path) else: path.unlink(missing_ok=True) for path in site.glob("pip-*.dist-info"): shutil.rmtree(path) pip_pkg = site / "pip" if pip_pkg.exists(): shutil.rmtree(pip_pkg) subprocess.check_call( [ sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "--disable-pip-version-check", "--no-cache-dir", "--no-index", "--find-links", wheelhouse, f"pip=={version}", "-t", str(site), ], stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, ) """ def _stable_version(version: str) -> Version | None: try: parsed = Version(version) except InvalidVersion: return None if parsed.is_prerelease or parsed.is_devrelease: return None return parsed def _fetch_pip_versions() -> list[str]: with urllib.request.urlopen("https://pypi.org/pypi/pip/json") as response: data = json.load(response) versions: list[str] = [] for version in data["releases"]: parsed = _stable_version(version) if parsed is not None and parsed >= MIN_VERSION: versions.append(version) return session venv and list tests.""" out = session.run( "python", "-c", """\ import importlib mod = importlib.import_module("tests.functional.test_install_extras") names = sorted( name for name, obj in test_install_extras.py: {', '.join(test_names)}") versions = _resolve_versions(list(session.posargs)) session.log(f"Testing {len(versions)} pip version(s)") plugin_dir = title: pip show command builds the installed-files list even without --files
body:
`pip show <pkg>` only prints installed files when `--files` is passed, but `search_packages_info()` always calls `iter_declared_entries()` and sorts the result for every matched distribution. that work is discarded in the default output.

the cost isn't a fixed per-package overhead; it scales with the number of entries in each package's `RECORD`, so it's most visible for large packages or when showing several at once.

`pip show` could gather installed files only when `--files` is set, while direct callers of `search_packages_info()` keep today's behavior by default.

**Benchmark**

same venv for both runs, switching only the pip source via PYTHONPATH. 2 warmups, 11 measured runs, median.

```text
# single
pip show Django
    baseline=0.1291s patched=0.1062s delta=0.0228s

# 3 dist
pip show Django scikit-learn scipy
    baseline=0.1447s patched=0.1141s delta=0.0305s

# 5 dist
pip show Django scikit-learn scipy numpy sympy
    baseline=0.1521s patched=0.1144s delta=0.0377s
```

title: Feedback / Suggestion: trust_env should not default to True unconditionally, or allow a way to configure it to False to prevent forced SOCKS dependencies.
body:
### What's the problem this feature will solve?

When users work on a clean Python environment behind system-wide SOCKS proxies (e.g., VPNs that automatically inject global `ALL_PROXY="socks://..."` variables), running pip fails immediately with a fatal error: `ERROR: Could not install packages due to an OSError: Missing dependencies for SOCKS support`.

Because pip implicitly maps `trust_env=True` on its underlying session by default, it enforces an unresolvable "chicken-and-egg" paradox:
1. `pip` refuses to connect anywhere because `pysocks` is not installed.
2. The user cannot use `pip install pysocks` to fix it because pip terminates immediately before communicating with the index server.

Furthermore, even if the user explicitly clears the local configuration via `pip config set global.proxy ""`, pip still trusts the environment variables anyway and crashes, completely ignoring the user's intent to switch to a direct connection.

### Describe the solution you'd like

We should provide a way to disable `trust_env` natively from configuration or automatically handle missing conditional SOCKS dependencies.

#### Proposed Solution A:
Allow an explicit flag or config block to set `trust_env = False` (e.g., `pip install --no-proxy-env` or `global.trust_env = false` in `pip.conf`). When disabled, pip should strictly ignore OS-level proxy environment variables like `ALL_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, and `HTTPS_PROXY`.

#### Proposed Solution B:
If `pysocks` is missing and a SOCKS scheme proxy is derived from the OS environment, pip should gracefully fall back to a direct connection with a non-blocking warning (e.g., `WARNING: SOCKS proxy skipped due to missing pysocks dependency, falling back to direct connection`) instead of halting with a fatal `OSError`.

Additionally, setting `global.proxy = ""` in `pip.conf` should automatically cascade and force `trust_env = False` for proxy evaluation.

### Alternative Solutions

* **Manual Session Variables Purge:** Users have to manually type `$env:all_proxy=""` (Windows PowerShell) or `unset ALL_PROXY` (Linux) inside every single active terminal session before triggering pip. This is extremely tedious and disrupts standard developer workflows.
* **The `--proxy=""` Hack:** Passing an empty proxy parameter via CLI bypasses `trust_env` but forces users to explicitly type it out every time. It cannot be cleanly globalized across different shells without environment modification.

### Additional context

* This relates heavily to the underlying discussion on **PR #13051** (Add `--no-proxy-env` Option), which introduces the argument to toggle `session.trust_env = False`.
* It builds on the consistency introduced by **PR #11091** (Make proxy parameter override environment proxy), which established precedent for changing `trust_env` behaviors under specific parameter contexts.

title: Optimize uninstall path compaction
body:
### What's the problem?

`pip._internal.req.req_uninstall.compact()` currently checks each candidate path against every previously-kept shorter path when reducing uninstall path listings. For uninstall inputs with many nested paths under package directories, this can lead to a large number of repeated prefix checks.

This is visible in the uninstall display/rename path, where `compact()` is used after collecting paths from uninstall records and directory walks.

### Expected improvement

The same result can be produced by keeping accepted prefixes in a set and walking each candidate path's parents until an accepted ancestor is found. That changes the core check from scanning all kept paths for every candidate to bounded parent traversal.

### Local benchmark

Synthetic uninstall-folder-shaped input:

- 40,500 paths under site-packages-like package directories
- compacted result: 500 paths
- same output digest before/after

Results on my machine:

```text
main:   median 0.418757s
branch: median 0.017444s
```

### Notes

I did not find an existing issue specifically tracking this `compact()` prefix-scan behavior. Issue #10175 also mentions slow uninstall behavior, but appears to cover a different user-visible problem.

title: pip show recomputes reverse dependency data for each requested package
body:
`pip show` currently computes `Required-by` separately for each queried package.

For a command like:

```console
python -m pip show pkg-a pkg-b pkg-c
```

`search_packages_info()` scans installed distributions once to build the installed package map, then for each queried package it calls `_get_requiring_packages()`, which scans all installed distributions again and parses each distribution's dependencies.

This makes the dependency scan scale roughly with:

```text
number of queried packages * number of installed distributions
```

Instead, `pip show` could precompute the reverse dependency mapping once while walking installed distributions, then reuse that mapping for each queried package.

title: `pip list` can parse METADATA twice per row with the importlib backend
body:
the default `pip list` columns output reads both `raw_name` and `raw_version` for every displayed distribution. (see [format_for_columns](https://github.com/pypa/pip/blob/73ac3f521dc53ff42f8a084cf3ac930163e8d63a/src/pip/_internal/commands/list.py#L357-L360))

with the importlib backend, `raw_name` goes through pip's cached metadata object, but `raw_version` goes through `importlib.metadata.Distribution.version`. that can parse the same `METADATA` again for each row.

See CPython's `Distribution.version` and `Distribution.metadata`:
- [`DIstribution.metadata`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/3.14/Lib/importlib/metadata/__init__.py#L449-L471) property
- [`Distribution.version`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/3.14/Lib/importlib/metadata/__init__.py#L484-L486) property

I think `raw_version` property can reuse pip's cached metadata object instead.

title: `IncompleteRead` exception crashes pip instantly, bypassing the built-in download resumption logic
body: ### Description When `pip download` encounters a sudden network disruption mid-transfer, the underlying network layer throws a protocol exception, such as `http.client.IncompleteRead`. Because this exception is not gracefully intercepted during the stream-reading phase, it instantly crashes the entire application execution context. As a result, `pip` immediately aborts the operation, completely bypassing its own downstream self-healing mechanisms (`_attempt_resumes_or_redownloads` / `_http_get_resume`) which were explicitly designed to issue HTTP Range requests and resume incomplete transfers. ### Expected behavior `pip` should recognize the stream-reading failure as a recoverable network event. Instead of crashing, it should transition the current download state safely into the resumption flow, allowing the client to utilize standard HTTP `206 Partial Content` handshakes to patch and complete the missing chunks seamlessly. ### pip version 26.1.1 ### Python version 3.13 ### OS Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS ### How to Reproduce 1. Save the following script as `server.py` and run it locally. This mock registry serves a 100MB fake package but intentionally cuts the connection via a hard TCP `RST` signal exactly after delivering 10MB to trigger an `IncompleteRead` on the client side: ```python import os import socket import re from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer # Definitive test asset (Simulating a 100MB heavy wheel) FAKE_FILE_SIZE = 100 * 1024 * 1024 WHEEL_FILENAME = "test_package-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl" # Global session/connection tracker connection_count = 0 class HellMockRegistryHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def do_GET(self): global connection_count # 1. Standard PEP-503 Simple Repository API routing if self.path in ["/simple/test-package/", "/simple/test-package"]: self.send_response(200) self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/html; charset=utf-8") self.end_headers() html = f'{WHEEL_FILENAME}' self.wfile.write(html.encode('utf-8')) return # 2. Heavy wheel payload stream distribution routing if self.path == f"/packages/{WHEEL_FILENAME}": connection_count += 1 range_header = self.headers.get("Range") print(f"\n⚡ [Session #{connection_count}] Inbound request captured!") start_byte = 0 # Inspecting HTTP Range headers for chunk resumption validations if range_header: match = re.match(r"bytes=(\d+)-", range_header) if match: start_byte = int(match.group(1)) print(f" 🎯 [RESUME BRANCH] Pip requesting offset from {start_byte // (1024*1024)}MB.") self.send_response(206) self.send_header("Content-Range", f"bytes {start_byte}-{FAKE_FILE_SIZE-1}/{FAKE_FILE_SIZE}") else: print(f" 🆕 [FRESH BRANCH] Pip initiating cold download from 0MB.") self.send_response(200) # Providing matching tokens to trick pip's conditional headers validation self.send_header("ETag", '"hell-mock-999"') self.send_header("Last-Modified", "Wed, 18 Jun 2026 00:00:00 GMT") remaining_bytes = FAKE_FILE_SIZE - start_byte self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream") self.send_header("Content-Length", str(remaining_bytes)) self.end_headers() # ---------------------------------------------------- # MALICIOUS SLICING: Enforce connection drop after 10MB # ---------------------------------------------------- MAX_TRANSMIT = 10 * 1024 * 1024 # 10MB threshold limit chunk_size = 64 * 1024 bytes_sent_this_session = 0 try: while bytes_sent_this_session < remaining_bytes: self.wfile.write(b"\x00" * min(chunk_size, remaining_bytes - bytes_sent_this_session)) bytes_sent_this_session += chunk_size # Connection severance trigger if bytes_sent_this_session >= MAX_TRANSMIT: current_total = start_byte + bytes_sent_this_session print(f" 💥 [SOCKET KILL] Pushed {bytes_sent_this_session // (1024*1024)}MB this session. Stream completed.") except Exception as e: print(f" [EXCEPTION] Stream transfer interrupted: {e}") return self.send_error(404, "Not Found") if __name__ == '__main__': print("==================================================") print(" Mock Pip Server (Hell Mode) active on port 8080") print("==================================================") HTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', 8080), HellMockRegistryHandler).serve_forever() ``` 2. title: (correctness): conflict checks are order-dependent when building the affected package whitelist
body:
`pip install`'s post-resolution conflict check builds a whitelist of packages to check: the packages being installed/upgraded and their direct dependents.

That whitelist is currently order-dependent because `_create_whitelist()` checks dependency names against `packages_affected`, which is mutated while iterating over installed packages.

For example:

```text
root -> middle -> leaf
```

If `leaf` is installed/upgraded, `middle` should be included as a direct dependent. `root` should not be included under the current policy, but depending on installed distribution iteration order it may be included after `middle` is added to `packages_affected`.

The check should compare dependencies against the frozen `would_be_installed` set so the whitelist remains direct-only and deterministic.

title: Arbitrary file deletion via path traversal in `RECORD` during `pip uninstall`
body:
### Description

`pip uninstall` can delete files outside a package's own installation directory because of an unvalidated path-traversal in distribution metadata.

When pip uninstalls a distribution, it reads the file paths listed in that distribution's `RECORD` (or legacy `installed-files.txt`) and joins each entry to the install location to decide what to delete. Those entries come from the package's own metadata and are not constrained to the directories the package installed into. An entry such as `../../../../<some path>` therefore resolves to a location outside the install tree.

`UninstallPathSet._permitted()` in `pip/_internal/req/req_uninstall.py` only restricts paths to `sys.prefix` **when running inside a virtualenv**. For system and `--user` installs it returns `True` for everything, so no containment check is applied and the out-of-tree path is scheduled for removal.

Impact: a package can cause `pip uninstall` (or an upgrade/reinstall, which uninstalls the old version first) to delete arbitrary files writable by the user running pip. This is silent file loss, not a crash. I have reproduced the full
chain against current `main`.


### Expected behavior

`pip uninstall` should only remove files within the directories the distribution actually installed into (its install scheme directories: purelib, platlib, scripts, headers, data, plus its own metadata location). Any `RECORD` /
`installed-files.txt` entry that resolves outside those directories should be refused and reported (added to the "would not remove" list), never deleted regardless of whether pip is running inside a virtualenv.

### pip version

26.2.dev0 (reproduced on current main); the unsafe code path exists in all currently released versions

### Python version

3.10 (issue is platform and Python-version independent)

### OS

Windows 11 (also reproducible on Linux/macOS the logic is OS-independent)

### How to Reproduce

The file paths listed in a distribution's `RECORD` are trusted and joined to the install location at uninstall time without checking they stay inside the package's own install directories. A package can therefore list a path that escapes its install tree, and `pip uninstall` will delete that file.

1. Create a victim file outside site-packages, e.g. `secret/victim.txt`.
2. Build a wheel (`evilpkg-1.0`) whose `evilpkg-1.0.dist-info/RECORD` contains a  relative traversal entry that points at that victim file, e.g. a line:  `../secret/victim.txt,,`  (this path is NOT a real file shipped in the wheel).
3. In a non-virtualenv environment (a system or `--user` install), install it:
   `pip install evilpkg-1.0-py3-none-any.whl`
   The traversal entry is carried verbatim into the installed RECORD on disk.
4. Uninstall it:
   `pip uninstall -y evilpkg`
5. Observe that `secret/victim.txt` — a file outside the package's install
   directory — has been deleted.

Root cause: `UninstallPathSet._permitted()` in `pip/_internal/req/req_uninstall.py` only constrains paths to `sys.prefix` when running inside a virtualenv; outside a virtualenv it returns True for everything, so no boundary is enforced on RECORD-declared paths.


### Output

## output with unpatched pip
$ python -m pip install --user --no-warn-script-location evilpkg-1.0-py3-none-any.whl
Processing .../evilpkg-1.0-py3-none-any.whl
Installing collected packages: evilpkg
Successfully installed evilpkg-1.0

### the traversal entry survived into the installed RECORD:
$ grep victim .../site-packages/evilpkg-1.0.dist-info/RECORD
../../../../Local/Temp/vuln_vs8q7ba6/victim.txt,,

### victim exists BEFORE uninstall: True
$ python -m pip uninstall -y evilpkg
Found existing installation: evilpkg 1.0
Uninstalling evilpkg-1.0:
  Successfully uninstalled evilpkg-1.0

### victim exists AFTER uninstall: False
>>> DELETED (out-of-tree file destroyed)

## output with patched pip
$ python -m pip uninstall -y evilpkg
Found existing installation: evilpkg 1.0
Uninstalling evilpkg-1.0:
  Successfully uninstalled evilpkg-1.0
WARNING: Ignoring entry that points outside the installation of evilpkg: c:\users\akibs\appdata\local\temp\vuln_5llnjf3u\victim.txt

### victim exists AFTER uninstall: True
>>> survived

title: raise_for_status relies on HTTP reason phrase, which is unreliable in practice
body:
### Problem

`pip._internal.network.utils.raise_for_status` builds its error detail from `resp.reason` — the HTTP reason phrase. This produces unhelpful errors like:

```
403 Client Error: Forbidden for url: https://...
```

even when the server has a specific, actionable explanation to give.

The reason phrase is an unreliable channel for this:

- **RFC 7230 §6.1 tells clients to ignore it**: *"A client SHOULD ignore the reason-phrase content."* The spec treats it as a human-readable hint, not a structured field.
- **Servers omit it by default**: Apache Tomcat 8.5+ and Jetty 9.4+ both send an empty reason phrase on HTTP/1.1 responses out of the box, aligning with HTTP/2 which removes the field entirely (RFC 7540 §8.1.2.4).
- **No enforced semantics**: servers use it inconsistently; proxies may replace it with a generic value.

### Proposed fix

Read the `X-Error-Message` response header when present on a 4xx or 5xx response and use its value as the error detail instead of `resp.reason`. Servers that do not send the header see no change in behaviour.

### Existing implementations

Other package ecosystems already use this header for exactly this purpose:

- **Hugging Face Hub** — reads `X-Error-Message` in [`huggingface_hub/utils/_http.py`](https://github.com/huggingface/huggingface_hub/blob/main/src/huggingface_hub/utils/_http.py). The HF API server has emitted this header for years.
- **RubyGems** — `gem` was updated to read `X-Error-Message` in [ruby/rubygems#9270](https://github.com/rubygems/rubygems/pull/9270) (released in 4.1.0).
- **NuGet** — uses `X-NuGet-Warning` (same pattern: custom header, human-readable string) defined in [`ProtocolConstants.cs`](https://github.com/NuGet/NuGet.Client/blob/dev/src/NuGet.Core/NuGet.Protocol/ProtocolConstants.cs).

Adopting the same convention means a server can send one header that surfaces actionable errors across multiple clients.

title: requests/urllib3 vendored in pip 25.1.1 truncates HTTP responses on Python 3.14.4
body:
## Environment
- Python: 3.14.4
- pip: 25.1.1 (venv)
- OS: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS
- OpenSSL: 3.5.5

## Error
json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Unterminated string starting at: line 1 column 40853 (char 40852)

Full traceback shows the error at `collector.py:231` in `parse_links` when doing `json.loads(page.content)`.

## Root Cause

The vendored `requests 2.32.3` (which wraps `urllib3 1.26.20`) truncates HTTP responses at **40960 bytes** when used with Python 3.14.4. Direct `http.client` and `urllib3` work correctly (full response of ~146KB is received).

This breaks pip entirely — it cannot install any package because it can't parse the JSON simple API response from PyPI.

## Workaround / Fix

Install a newer pip version manually by downloading the wheel directly with `urllib`:

python3 -c "
import urllib.request
url = 'https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/3a/eb/fea4d1d51c49832120f7f285d07306db3960f423a2612c6057caf3e8196f/pip-26.1.1-py3-none-any.whl'
resp = urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url))
with open('/tmp/pip-26.1.1-py3-none-any.whl', 'wb') as f:
    f.write(resp.read())

title: --require-hashes does not apply to build-system dependencies, undocumented bypass
body:
## Summary

`pip install --require-hashes` does not enforce hash checking for build-system dependencies declared in `[build-system].requires`. Users who rely on `--require-hashes` for supply-chain integrity have no way to discover this from the documentation.

This issue is related to #13983 . That issue covers pip not reconciling PEP 658 sidecar metadata against the wheel after download. 
The PSRT's recommended mitigation for that finding was `--require-hashes`, which this issue shows does not provide complete coverage.

## Root Cause

**File:** `src/pip/_internal/build_env.py` 
**Class:** `InprocessBuildEnvironmentInstaller`

The installer hard-codes `require_hashes=False` when fetching build deps, when a user runs:

`pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt`

against a requirements file that includes an sdist, that sdist's `[build-system].requires` dependencies are fetched and executed without any hash verification, regardless of what the user has pinned.

## Impact

`--require-hashes` is the primary mechanism pip users rely on to protect against supply chain attacks. A developer who reads the documentation, pins all their dependencies with hashes, and runs `--require-hashes` has a reasonable expectation that nothing runs during install without being hash-verified first. That expectation is wrong whenever an sdist is involved.

The build backend executes during `prepare_metadata_for_build_wheel()` with full access to the process environment: CI/CD tokens, cloud credentials, SSH agent sockets, database URLs, and any other secrets present at install time. A compromised or malicious build dependency resolves and runs before the top-level package is installed, and there is no user-visible signal that this happened outside the scope of `--require-hashes` protection.

Potential attack path: a typosquatted or dependency-confused build backend name in `[build-system].requires` resolves and executes on the first `pip install --require-hashes` run against a fresh sdist. The user sees the top-level install succeed. Nothing in the output indicates that an unhashed package ran during the build phase.

We validated it end-to-end: a build backend executed, read the full process environment, and transmitted it over a network connection while `--require-hashes` was active for the top-level requirements. pip exited 0.

The documentation for `--require-hashes` contains no mention of this limitation. Users who set up `--require-hashes` specifically because they are worried about supply chain attacks are the most likely to install from sdists with custom build backends, and the least likely to know this protection does not extend to them.

## Proposed Fix

Either: 
1. Extend hash checking to build deps. The TODO comment acknowledges this is the right long-term fix. It is a breaking change because it requires users to also pin build deps, but a migration path (warning first, enforce later) is feasible. 
2. At minimum, document the limitation clearly in the `--require-hashes` help text and docs so users know their install is not fully covered when sdists are involved.

## Disclosure Note

This was identified during security research into pip's integrity model and discussed with the Python Security Response Team (PSRT) in April 2026 as a solution for #13983 . The PSRT deferred the question of build dependency hash enforcement to the pip maintainers. 

## Environment

Confirmed on pip 25.1.1 and pip 26.0.1 / Python 3.13.5 / macOS.

**Reported by:** Dewank Pant and Shruti Lohani

title: pip does not reconcile PEP 658 sidecar .metadata against wheel METADATA after download
body:
## Summary

When pip uses a PEP 658 `.metadata` sidecar file for dependency resolution, it never verifies that the sidecar matches the canonical `METADATA` embedded in the downloaded wheel. pip has both files available after the wheel is fetched, but the comparison never happens.

## Root Cause

**File:** `src/pip/_internal/operations/prepare.py` 

**Function:** `_fetch_metadata_using_link_data_attr()` (~line 389)

pip downloads the sidecar, parses it into a `BaseDistribution`, and stores it as `req._distribution`, the permanent resolution-time source of truth. Later, when the wheel is downloaded and its sha256 verified, the code never extracts the wheel's embedded `METADATA` to compare `Requires-Dist`, `Requires-Python`, or `Provides-Extra` against what the sidecar declared.

The only consistency check performed is a case-insensitive `Name` comparison. Version, dependencies, and extras are never reconciled.

PEP 658 states: 

> The metadata MUST be identical to the metadata in the distribution file.

pip does not enforce this invariant even when it has both files in hand.

## Impact

On a self-hosted index where sidecar files are not hash-protected, a common configuration in enterprise PyPI mirrors, S3-backed indexes, and internal Artifactory or Nexus deployments, this gap enables a silent supply chain attack without the user ever knowing.

A concrete attack path: an attacker with write access to artifact storage (an S3 bucket, a blob store, a CDN edge cache) but no access to the index page or wheel files serves a tampered `.metadata` sidecar that declares `Requires-Dist: attacker-pkg`. pip resolves and builds `attacker-pkg` as a transitive dependency of a legitimate, unmodified wheel whose sha256 passes. The attacker's build backend executes during `pip install` with full access to the process environment, CI/CD tokens, cloud credentials, SSH agent sockets, and transmits them to an attacker-controlled endpoint. pip exits 0. No new file appears on disk that a scanner would flag. No unexpected network connection appears in logs. No version number changes. The injected package arrives as a seemingly legitimate transitive dependency.

`pip install --report` records the tampered sidecar's `requires_dist`, not the installed wheel's canonical metadata, so the audit trail is also wrong.

We confirmed the full exploit chain end-to-end: tampered sidecar served alongside an unmodified wheel, build backend fired during `prepare_metadata_for_build_wheel()`, credentials exfiltrated over TCP, pip exited 0 with the victim seeing only standard spinner output at default verbosity. The wheel's sha256 matched throughout.

The fix is contained and pip already has everything it needs: the wheel is on disk at the point where reconciliation would happen. Checking `Requires-Dist` from the wheel against what the sidecar declared is a single function addition.

## Proposed Fix

After the wheel is downloaded, extract its embedded `METADATA` and compare `Requires-Dist`, `Requires-Python`, and `Provides-Extra` against the sidecar-derived distribution stored in `req._distribution`. Abort or emit a clear warning on mismatch.

## Disclosure Note

This was originally reported to the Python Security Response Team (security@python.org) in April 2026. The PSRT reviewed it and determined it falls outside pip's current security threat model, which assumes index trust, but recommended opening a public issue as a hardening improvement. Full disclosure thread available if needed.

## Environment

Confirmed on pip 25.1.1 and pip 26.0.1 / Python 3.13.5 / macOS.

**Reported by:** Dewank Pant and Shruti Lohani

Hey there 👋

We're adding inline types to Requests (psf/requests#7272), targeting a release in the coming weeks.

I've started testing against pip and wanted to note a couple things:
1. pip currently vendors its own requests.pyi stubs redirecting to typeshed. Those differ slightly from what we'll be shipping. There's also a [mypy config](https://github.com/pypa/pip/blob/cc6b082d6b9350d96c5a24337b12b7a42846c410/pyproject.toml#L304-L306) ignoring types from Requests by default.

Would the team be open to migrating off current configs to use Requests' inline types directly? My initial check shows ~14 errors in _internal/network files, but most are legitimate fixes. I can put up a draft PR against a pre-release next week to get feedback and have it ready for the final 2.34.0 release. Otherwise, we can do the vendor update as one body of work and typing as a second.

Happy to defer if you'd rather stick with stubs for now too. Let me know what the preferred approach would be.

```
[[packages]]
```

title: Would pip consider a plugin hook for custom project config file discovery?
body:
### What's the problem this feature will solve?

pip currently hardcodes detection of `pyproject.toml` and `setup.py` in `is_installable_dir()` and `load_pyproject_toml()`. There's no way for a third-party language toolchain to register an additional config file format without forking pip or shipping a redundant shim `pyproject.toml`.

### Describe the solution you'd like

A small plugin API - similar to the existing `VcsSupport.register()` pattern - where tools can register:

- A detector: `(directory: str) -> bool`
- A loader: returns the existing BuildSystemDetails namedtuple (PEP 517 backend info)

Registration via entry points:
```
[project.entry-points."pip.project_config"]
mytool = "mytool.build:ConfigPlugin"
```
This would be purely additive - no behavior change for existing projects.

### Alternative Solutions

The current workaround is a boilerplate `pyproject.toml` shim that points to a custom PEP 517 backend, which then reads the real config file. It works but forces every project to carry a meaningless file just to satisfy pip's hardcoded check.

### Additional context

Before writing a full proposal, I wanted to check if this direction is something the pip team would consider. Happy to write a detailed spec / draft PR if there's interest.

A Python-transpiled language that already hooks into Python's import system cleanly via `sys.meta_path`. We're looking for the same clean integration at the pip layer.

title: Add an explicit AI policy to our documentation
body:
As noted in #13825, we're starting to get AI-generated contributions. In order to ensure our limited maintainer bandwidth isn't overwhelmed, and to protect us from any ownership or licensing concerns over submitted code, I suggest that we explicitly adopt and document an AI policy. My strong preference is for something based on the `attrs` policy - https://github.com/python-attrs/attrs/blob/main/.github/AI_POLICY.md. In my view, this takes the correct stance, focusing on ensuring that every PR has a human contributor associated, and that contributor takes full resaponsibility for the technical and legal/ownership aspects of their contribution.

There are always going to be judgement calls involved - after all, LLMs *by design* produce plausible looking content - so the policy will of necessity be subject to interpretation. By choosing a policy that assumes good faith on the part of submitters, while still being clear that we *will* impose penalties like rejection or banning when necessary, I think we strike a reasonable balance.

I have created #13826 as a starting point for discussion.

title: Consider speciesist language in documentation
body:
## Description

Proposing that pip's documentation guidelines consider speciesist language — animal-derived idioms that normalize violence toward animals — alongside the Python community's existing inclusive language efforts.

The PSF diversity statement and CPython's master→main migration demonstrate the Python ecosystem's commitment to inclusive terminology. Speciesist language is the next category being addressed across the industry.

## Common terms and alternatives

| Avoid | Use instead |
|---|---|
| "kill two birds with one stone" | "accomplish two things at once" |
| "beat a dead horse" | "belabor the point" |
| "monkey patch" | "runtime patch" |
| "guinea pig" | "test subject" |
| "canary release" | "preview release" |

These alternatives are also more precise and accessible to non-native English speakers.

## References

- Hagendorff et al. 2023, "Speciesist bias in AI," *AI and Ethics* ([DOI: 10.1007/s43681-023-00380-w](https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-023-00380-w))
- [Open-Paws/speciesist-language-scanner](https://github.com/Open-Paws/speciesist-language-scanner) — automated detection tooling for multiple linters
- This follows the same trajectory as master→main and whitelist→allowlist

This is about awareness for new writing, not a retroactive overhaul.

title: Making vendored libraries optional and bootstrapping pip?
body:
In the DPO [discussion](https://discuss.python.org/t/adopting-toml-1-1/105624) about TOML 1.1 and the PR discussion in https://github.com/pypa/pip/pull/13750 it was brought up the downsides of vendoring with regards to bootstrapping.

Unpatched, pip currently doesn't allow for any of the vendored libraries to be removed, and acheive minimal functionality.

I am wondering, would it make sense that to achieve the goal that we could delete the directory `src/pip/_vendor` and still have some minimal install functionality continue to work? I imagine bootstrapping would look like:

```
python src/pip/__main__.py install {path to vendorless pip source tree} 
```

Some steps that involve vendoring, either by calling `python -m pip install vendoring` and then `python -m vendoring ...`, or having a vendoring script with less dependencies. And finally:


```
python -m pip install --force {path to pip source tree now with vendored libraries}
```

Is there a desire for this? To guarantee such bootstrapping capabilities? 

I'm not advocating for it, but I am trying to understand how much we should worry or care about bootstrapping in the pip project.

title: one possible solution to "An existing connection was forcibly closed by the remote host" when the issue comes from kaspersky
body:
## Foreword:

*I wanted to add this to #12406, but the issue's locked*

----

## What happened?

I was fiddling around with `pyinstaller`, when I decided to upgrade from Python 3.10.0 to 3.13.x. After uninstalling Python 3.10.0 and generally cleaning up a bit "while I'm at it", I installed Python 3.13.11 and ran `pip install numpy`, only to be told:

`
WARNING: Retrying (Retry(total=4, connect=None, read=None, redirect=None, status=None)) after connection broken by 'ProtocolError('Connection aborted.', ConnectionResetError(10054, 'An existing connection was forcibly closed by the remote host', None, 10054, None))': /simple/numpy/`

I tried so many suggestions I could feel my hairline receding, until I noticed the: "only turn off the firewall after the OS has shut down completely" setting in Kaspersky Internet Security. Thus, I turned off the firewall first before deactivating Kaspersky and rebooting aaand whadduyouknow, I could install packages with pip again!

## The solution

"Deactivate the firewall, then Kaspersky and reboot" every time I want to install something isn't exactly practical, so I looked deeper into Kaspersky and found this post: https://forum.kaspersky.com/topic/kaspersky-is-blocking-python-from-accessing-the-internet-32579/

Following these steps listed in the accepted answer fixed the problem:

- Make sure Windows Hidden files, is checked/ticked, refer: View hidden files and folders in Windows
- Open Kaspersky app, select Settings⚙, select General, uncheck Enable Self-Defense, select Save, select Yes - to confirm the action.
- Exit Kaspersky app - on the Windows taskbar or hidden icons, rightclick the Kaspersky icon, select Exit.
- Go to folder C:\ProgramData\Kaspersky Lab\AVP21.3\Report\ and delete the contents = all files and folders.
- Start Kaspersky app.
- Enable Self-Defense.
- Shutdown the computer, using Shutdown, not Restart, power on, login.

----

This drove me <ins>nuts</ins> and took two days, so I wanted to share it for others, when Kaspersky actually IS the problem, but doesn't SEEM to be, because temporarily deactivating it doesn't work.

title: Add --metadata-only flag to pip download for extracting packages metadata
body:
### What's the problem this feature will solve?

This proposal introduces a --metadata-only flag for pip's download command, enabling users to fetch package metadata without downloading complete package distributions. This addresses critical workflows in dependency analysis, security auditing, and CI/CD optimization while significantly reducing bandwidth usage and download times.

Currently, pip users face several limitations when working with package metadata:

1. **Inefficient Dependency Inspection**: Downloading entire packages (often hundreds of MB) just to inspect dependencies or metadata
2. **Wasted Resources**: CI/CD pipelines downloading full packages before compatibility checks
3. **Network Constraints**: Slow or metered connections make exploratory package analysis prohibitively expensive
4. **Security Auditing Friction**: Security teams need to audit metadata across hundreds of packages, requiring massive downloads
5. **No Planning Phase**: Users cannot preview installation requirements before committing disk space



## Proposed solution:

Add a `--metadata-only` flag to pip download:

```bash
# Download only metadata
pip download --metadata-only django

# Inspect dependencies without downloading packages
pip download --metadata-only --dry-run django

# Save metadata for offline analysis
pip download --metadata-only -d ./metadata django

# Batch metadata download for security auditing
pip download --metadata-only -r requirements.txt -d ./audit
```

## Technical Approach:

1. **For Wheels**: Extract only `.dist-info` directory from wheel archives (PEP 427)
2. **For Source Distributions**: Fetch metadata via PEP 658 (metadata in index) when available
3. **Fallback Strategy**: Gracefully handle packages without metadata URLs
4. **Cache Integration**: Store metadata separately from package cache

## Real World Scenarios:

### 1. Security Auditing
**Scenario**: Security team audits 200+ packages monthly for compliance

```bash
# Download only metadata for all dependencies
pip download --metadata-only -r production.txt -d ./audit-jan-2026

# Audit metadata for security issues (licenses, versions, dependencies)
python audit_script.py ./audit-jan-2026
```

**Impact**: 
- **Before**: ~2 GB download, 30 minutes
- **After**: ~5 MB download, 30 seconds
- **Savings**: 99.75% bandwidth reduction, 60x faster

### 2. CI/CD Pipeline Optimization
**Scenario**: Multi-stage CI pipeline with compatibility checks

```bash
# Stage 1: Fast compatibility check (seconds, not minutes)
pip download --metadata-only -r requirements.txt --python-version 3.11

# Stage 2: Only if Stage 1 passes, download actual packages
pip download -r requirements.txt
```

**Impact**: Fail-fast approach saves CI minutes and costs

### Alternative Solutions

Download the whole package.

### Additional context

Other modern package managers already provide similar functionality:

- **npm**: `npm view` fetches metadata without downloading
- **cargo**: `cargo metadata` provides dependency information
- **go**: `go list -m` shows module information
- **poetry**: Resolves dependencies without downloading packages

This feature brings pip closer to feature parity with modern package management tools.

title: Unpin versions of dependencies as a consnumer
body:
### What's the problem this feature will solve?

When integrating Python packages, users frequently run into dependency resolution issues caused by *strictly pinned transitive dependencies*, for example:

- `pytest==7.3.1`
- `pytest<=7.3`

These pins are often added with good intentions. At the time a dependency is released, a newer version (e.g. `pytest==7.4.0`) may not yet exist, and maintainers want to be conservative because future releases *might* introduce breaking changes.

However, in practice, newer releases often remain compatible. Once a new version is published, the pin remains unchanged until the dependency maintainer updates and releases a new version. As a result, **end users are blocked**, even when they know (or have tested) that newer versions work perfectly fine.

This makes users dependent on the release cadence and responsiveness of upstream maintainers for issues that are often low-risk.

Summarized: Strict dependency pins are often reasonable at release time, but they can become unnecessary blockers later on. Providing a supported, explicit way for consumers to override or ignore specific transitive dependency constraints would significantly improve flexibility and usability, while still preserving safety and transparency.


--- 
Today, users have only a few options, all of which are suboptimal:

- Fork the dependency and relax the pin
- Vendor and patch the package locally
- Install with `--no-deps` and manually manage dependencies
- Switch to another dependency management tool with partial override support

These approaches:
- Increase maintenance burden
- Add complexity as multiple `pip install` commands must be run one after each other in correct order
- error-prone as some dependencies might be missed
- 



### Describe the solution you'd like

Introduce a mechanism that allows **consumers** to explicitly ignore or override specific transitive dependency constraints.

This would give users a controlled, explicit way to say:

> “I acknowledge the risk and intentionally want to override this dependency constraint.”


Unpin dependency versions via new flag `--unpin unpin.txt`, whereby this file could look similar to this

```txt
some-package # unpin all dependencies of a package
other-package:pytest # unpin only a single dependency
```

### Alternative Solutions

1. Ignore a specific dependency constraint from a package in `requirements.txt`
```txt
some-package
!some-package:pytest
pytest>=7.4
```

This might be a breaking change, as current pip versions will not work with this requirements.txt anymore.
Therefore I think, this will not be accepted.

2. Inline annotation in `requirements.txt`
```txt
some-package  # ignore-dep: pytest
pytest>=7.4
```

This would not work in command line, so I think this is also not an acceptable solution.




### Additional context

I face this issue currently with codechecker in zephyr context:
Pinned versions: https://github.com/Ericsson/codechecker/blob/6e69da3270a5faec62511cb93007b1c3e67e7659/analyzer/requirements.txt

As a result it is not compatible when installing together with zephyr's `requirements.txt`:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/scripts/requirements.txt

title: Add warning when index or extra index returns HTTP 404 (e.g., due to invalid token)
body:
### What's the problem this feature will solve?

Currently, when pip attempts to install a package from a custom index or extra index URL and the server responds with HTTP 404, no explicit warning is shown. This can be misleading for users because in some cases (e.g., GitLab PyPI registry), a revoked, expired, or out-of-scope token causes the index endpoint to return 404 instead of 403 or 401.

Users may incorrectly assume the package does not exist, when in reality the authentication failed.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add a warning message (at least in `--verbose` mode) when:

* The primary index URL returns HTTP 404.
* Any extra index URL returns HTTP 404.

The warning should clarify that the issue might be due to authentication or configuration, not necessarily the absence of the package.

* Detect HTTP 404 responses during index fetching.
* Log a warning such as: `WARNING: Index URL returned 404 (Not Found): <index-url>. This may indicate an invalid token or misconfiguration.`


### Alternative Solutions

```
pip install non-existing-package --index-url https://httpbin.dev/status/400
```

### Additional context

Example Scenario

Using GitLab’s PyPI registry: `https://__token__:_BAD_TOKEN_@gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/<PID>/packages/pypi/simple`
If the provided token is invalid or expired, the endpoint returns 404.

Respect the max age cache control for simple API responses, with option to modify
body:
In https://github.com/pypa/pip/pull/5791 caching simple API responses was turned off, even if a max age cache control response was sent back, this solved one use case at the performance cost of everyone.

When doing multiple pip commands, especially ones that don't require downloading distributions, like pip lock, pip install --dry-run, and pip install where the distributions are already in cache, this contributes to a significant amount of the resolution time.

uv respects the the max age cache control and gives users a way to set their own values for the API and files: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/indexes/#customizing-cache-control-headers.

title: Implement a relative cooldown in `--exclude-newer`
body:
### What's the problem this feature will solve?

I think it would be great if `pip` implements a "cooldown" feature. This has been recently widely discussed in the security community after the `npm` being targetted by the `Shai-Hulud 2` malware, that cooldowns would be a great protection for - especially - open-source projects and libraries that do not necessary need to get the latest packages immediately.

Cooldown periods will give time to registry maintainers (both public `PyPI` and other registries) to perform necessary scans, security researchers reviews, AI tools, running sandboxed tests by security-focused 3rd-parties on new versions of packages release and increase the chance that malware will be detected before it is installed.

This article from @woodruffw https://blog.yossarian.net/2025/11/21/We-should-all-be-using-dependency-cooldowns describes the cooldown effects pretty well, and calls for everyone to use cooldowns.

It's easy with dependabot and renovate on CI, however there is also another vector of attack - locak workstations of developers where the install packages, and it would be great to have confguration and option to have cooldown period applied by default on those workstations.

Of course there is the `--exclude-newer` but it only has support for specifying the absolute date, not relative one. Of course you could do all the bash or zsh magic to calculate it, but that's not really an option if you would like to configure a default cooldown period.

UV already has a PR in progress about it https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/16814 after very deep discussion about it - and it aims to allow relative specification for the `--exclude-newer`, which I think is a very good idea.

It would be great to have such relative `--exclude-newer` in `pip` - both as command line and configurable default.

### Describe the solution you'd like

The `--exclude-newer` could accept other values than absolute timestamp - specifically relative time specification like '1 day`, `1 week`, `30 days`. 

### Alternative Solutions

Telling people to calculate the date and pass it to `--exclude-newer` in the absolute timestamp form. Unfortunately that does not achieve easily the "default behaviour" of specific cooldown period like 5 days.

### Additional context

https://blog.yossarian.net/2025/11/21/We-should-all-be-using-dependency-cooldowns

title: ConfigOptionParser: Incorrect splitting of quoted values and crash on callback without des
body:
### Description

# Description
I encountered two distinct issues within the `ConfigOptionParser._update_defaults` method while analyzing the configuration parsing logic.

**1. Incorrect splitting of configuration values (Logic Error)**
When an option is defined with `action="append"`, the `_update_defaults` method uses the default `str.split()` to parse the configuration string.
```python
# Current implementation
val = val.split()
```
This causes configuration values containing spaces (e.g., file paths on Windows or quoted strings) to be split incorrectly, even if they are quoted. For example, "C:\Program Files" becomes ['"C:\Program', 'Files"'] instead of ['C:\Program Files'].

2. Crash on callback options (Runtime Error) When an option is defined with action="callback" and does not specify a dest (which is valid in optparse if the callback handles logic internally), the code blindly adds option.dest (which is None) to the late_eval set.

```python
# Current implementation
elif option.action == "callback":
    assert option.callback is not None
    late_eval.add(option.dest)  # <--- Adds None to set
```
Later in the method, the code iterates over late_eval and calls getattr(self.values, key). If key is None, this raises a TypeError


### Expected behavior

_No response_

### pip version

main (current dev)

### Python version

3.10+

### OS

all

### How to Reproduce



**Reproduction Case 1 (Splitting Bug):**
1. Define a `ConfigOptionParser`.
2. Add an option: `parser.add_option("--includes", action="append", dest="includes")`.
3. Provide a configuration string in a config file: `includes = "path/one" "path/two with spaces"`.
4. **Current Result:** `['"path/one"', '"path/two', 'with', 'spaces"']` (Broken split)
5. **Expected Result:** `['path/one', 'path/two with spaces']`

**Reproduction Case 2 (Callback Crash):**
1. Define a `ConfigOptionParser`.
2. Define a dummy callback function.
3. Add an option: `parser.add_option("--run-me", action="callback", callback=dummy_cb, dest=None)`.
4. Initialize the parser and trigger `_update_defaults` via configuration loading.
5. **Result:** The application crashes with `TypeError: getattr(): attribute name must be string` when the parser attempts to access `self.values` using `None` as the key.

title: Drop Python 3.9 support
body:
We've been dropping Python 3.x support for the last couple of releases on the YY.1 release, I propose we continue this process.

In particular dropping Python 3.9 will allow pip to finally switch from urllib3 v1 to v2, and truststore will be enabled by default for all users.

Like with the previous release I suggest we keep the ruff `target-version` to the dropped version of Python, at least for one release: https://github.com/pypa/pip/blob/25.3/pyproject.toml#L206. This will validate no [breaking syntax](https://astral.sh/blog/ruff-v0.12.0#syntax-errors-emitted-by-the-python-compiler) for Python 3.9 in pip's internal code.

And I do wonder if we should have a separate (informal) policy for syntax breakage, compared to explicit support, given the tooling makes it quite easy.

title: Improve warning in pip install documentation
body:
The warning [here](https://github.com/pypa/pip/blob/5f8a352d1041818ec49e7ad8e3f27178c5322bd3/docs/html/cli/pip_install.rst?plain=1#L482) about a dependency confusion attack is ambiguous since it does not explicitly state which option is unsafe. The warning

>Using this option to search for packages ...

is sandwiched between two different pip install examples. Directly before the warning is an example with `--no-index` and `--find-links` while directly after is an example with `--extra-index-url`.

The warning could be understood to apply to either option.

A simple fix would be to change the language of the warning from

>Using this option to search for packages ...

title: Resolving rejects all wheels for a given version causing otherwise valid wheels to be missed.
body:
### Description

Given these wheels and dependencies:

```
root -> a == 1
root -> b == 1
b-1-py3-none-any.whl -> a == 2
b-1-py2.py3-none-any.whl -> a == 1
```

If you run a command like `pip install a==1 b==1` then whether or not the resolving succeeds or not depends on whether it "saw" `b-1-py3-none-any.whl` or `b-1-py2.py3-none-any.whl` first.

It appears that when resolvelib rejects the first `b 1` wheel it finds, it rejects `b==1` as a whole, even though the second wheel in that set might resolve fine.


### Expected behavior

I expect pip to select the wheel that makes the resolution able to succeed, or at least have consistent behavior regardless of which wheel it sees "first".

title: For pyproject.toml: standardized package versions overrides and per-package indexes
body:
### What's the problem this feature will solve?

Supporting flexible manual overrides, indexes et cetera is important because packaging bugs happen all the time, and not always end-users have ability to force maintainers to rconcile these problems upstream

### Describe the solution you'd like

E.g. uv supports the following:

1. overriding transitive package dependency to force-fix some packaging bugs
2. specify a per-package index (should only apply to resolving vllm and not other packages)

This is supported/tried in `uv`, it would be great to have pip standardize these features/sections in pyproject.toml (and ideally support them as well - without needing to rely on uv for these)

```toml
# pyproject.toml for installing reasonably nightly vllm with flash-attn
```
